Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, xin.chen@isye.gatech.edu \AUTHORfont \HD 150David Simchi-Levi \HD 06 \AFFfont Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Operations Research Center, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, dslevi@mit.edu; Mitch Daniels School of Business, Purdue University, dslevi@purdue.edu \HOOKtop \TITLEfont \HD 240 \theTITLE \HD 015 \theARTICLEAUTHORS \HOOKb \ABSfont Negotiation is a fundamental strategic interaction in management science, characterized by agents attempting to reach agreements while protecting private information, such as reservation costs and hidden valuations. A prevalent yet complex scenario involves a single seller negotiating concurrently with multiple buyers, each possessing heterogeneous, private budgets. In such settings, constrained by a limited number of communication turns, the seller must balance exploring the broader market to discover the highest valuation with concentrating sufficient turns on a single target buyer to secure the best possible outcome. Our analysis reveals a significant gap in standard Large Language Models (LLMs): while these models are linguistically proficient, they fail to act as effective economic decision-makers. Specifically, they exhibit a failure to explore the buyer pool, often fixating on the current highest bid rather than strategically investigating the market to discover latent high valuations. In this paper, we propose a specialized training recipe using Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). By anchoring the reward function to objective economic outcomes, the strategic balance between market discovery and surplus extraction emerges natively through the learning process. Our results demonstrate that the trained seller undergoes a multi-stage strategic evolution, learning to leverage price anchoring and strategic probing to identify more profitable counterparties. The agent extracts substantially higher surplus than frontier models by both improving its persuasive bargaining skills and consistently closing deals with high-value buyers. Finally, we show that our seller strategies generalize robustly to unseen buyer negotiation styles and budget distributions. \theFUNDING \theKEYWORDS \theSUBJECTCLASS \theAREAOFREVIEW \theMSCCLASS \theORMSCLASS \theHISTORY 1 Introduction Negotiation is a foundational process in management science and operations research, serving as the primary mechanism for value discovery and resource allocation in environments where prices are not static ( Simchi-Levi et al. 2005 , Backus et al. 2020 ) . In fields ranging from procurement and supply chain contracting to dispute resolution and online marketplaces, agents must strategically interact to coordinate and realize gains from trade ( Cachon and Lariviere 2001 , Desai and Purohit 2004 ) . Within management science literature, the analysis of these strategic interactions focuses heavily on aligning decentralized incentives and resolving information gaps between trading partners ( Nagarajan and Sošić 2008 , Lovejoy 2010 ) . A central challenge in any negotiation is that agents possess private information—specifically, a seller has a minimum cost they are willing to accept, and a buyer has a maximum budget they are willing to pay—which remains hidden from their counterpart ( Chatterjee and Samuelson 1983 ) . To capture meaningful value under these asymmetric conditions, a seller must maintain strict strategic discipline. This requires simultaneously enforcing a private cost boundary to prevent loss-making transactions, reading buyer signals to extract maximum market surplus, and effectively coordinating with the buyer to establish a common price point and close the deal. While classical literature often focuses on bilateral (one-on-one) trade ( Nash and others 1950 , Rubinstein 1982 , Chatterjee and Samuelson 1983 ) , a highly prevalent scenario in modern management is concurrent negotiation, where a single focal seller interacts simultaneously with multiple independent buyers across separate, sealed channels ( Backus et al. 2020 ) . This parallel structure is central to digital marketplaces like eBay and business-to-business procurement platforms, where a seller allocates an available asset or supply contract by negotiating across a pool of potential buyers ( Backus et al. 2020 ) . Crucially, because the seller operates under a limited communication capacity across these parallel channels, it faces a fundamental trade-off between exploration and exploitation. The seller cannot afford extended bargaining cycles with every participant; instead, it must balance broad market screening to identify the counterparty with the highest hidden valuation against concentrated, single-buyer bargaining to maximize surplus extraction. When deploying autonomous or automated agents in these settings to act as direct representatives of the firm, failing to locate the optimal partner or settling for thin margins with an early bidder results in an immediate loss of organizational value. To manage these concurrent negotiations at scale, firms are actively deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) as autonomous bargaining agents. In digital platforms like Facebook Marketplace, automated tools assist users by managing simultaneous price inquiries and drafting real-time offers across independent buyer channels ( Meta 2026 ) . Similarly, in enterprise procurement, retail leaders like Walmart utilize automated negotiation systems to execute binding contracts with thousands of tail-end suppliers, bypassing the capacity constraints of human purchasing teams ( Van Hoek et al. 2022 ) . However, these current implementations operate primarily as reactive text filters designed to minimize conversational friction ( Meta 2026 ) , rather than strategic revenue management systems ( Gallego and Hu 2014 ) . Faced with a limited communication budget, the agent’s primary task is not conversational fluency, but using the dialogue to screen hidden buyer valuations and protect profit margins by allocating communication efforts to the highest-value counterparties. Our analysis reveals a critical misalignment between this required strategic discipline and the operational behavior of generalist frontier models. While standard LLMs excel at maintaining conversational fluency, they typically exhibit an agreeableness bias, maximizing total deal volume at the expense of overall economic surplus ( Ouyang et al. 2022 , Perez et al. 2023 , Sharma et al. 2024 ) . Because these models are optimized via reinforcement learning from human feedback for politeness and cooperation, they are prone to making suboptimal concessions rather than investigating the buyer pool to discover latent high valuations. Consequently, this bias turns their conversational fluency into a financial liability, preventing the agent from maximizing captured surplus. This paper addresses these limitations. We make three primary contributions: 1. A concurrent negotiation framework for evaluating exploration-exploitation trade-offs (Section 3 ). We establish a structured environment where a seller negotiates concurrently against multiple buyers with diverse budgets through private, one-on-one communication channels. This setting allows us to measure an agent’s ability to balance the strategic discovery of high-budget buyers with focused bargaining to extract surplus under limited communication turns. 2. A behavioral analysis identifying the exploration failure in frontier LLMs (Section 5 ). We demonstrate that even state-of-the-art general-purpose models, including those with specialized reasoning capabilities, fail to maximize surplus in multi-buyer settings. Our results reveal a systematic tendency to settle for suboptimal deals by fixating on early high bids rather than investigating the broader buyer pool to identify buyers with higher private budgets. 3. A specialized training recipe for strategic agents using Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (Section 4 ). We demonstrate that Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can effectively bridge the gap between conversational fluency and strategic utility. Our formulation utilizes objective economic outcomes—specifically deal surplus—and strict instruction-following protocols to guide the learning process. Our results show that this approach enables the emergence of proactive market discovery mechanisms, such as diagnostic probing and price anchoring, allowing agents to identify profitable partners even when facing unfamiliar buyer behaviors and unseen budget distributions. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on negotiation in management science and LLM agents. Section 3 formalizes the concurrent bargaining environment as a Markov Decision Process and specifies the agent system. Section 4 analyzes the behavioral evolution and phase shifts observed during reinforcement learning training. Section 5 presents the in-distribution performance benchmarking results against frontier models, and Section 6 evaluates the strategic robustness and market generalization of our agent. Finally, Section 7 discusses the broader strategic implications of our findings, and Section 8 concludes the paper. 2 Related Work We organize the relevant literature into the following streams: negotiation in management science, the evaluation of LLMs as strategic agents, automated negotiation systems, reinforcement learning for language models, and the foundations of classical bargaining theory. 2.1 Negotiation in Management Science and Operations Negotiation serves as a fundamental mechanism for price discovery and supply chain coordination within management science, particularly when firms lack direct visibility into a partner’s private costs or reservation thresholds. Research in management science extensively evaluates these bargaining dynamics to optimize incentive alignment in procurement and capacity contracting under asymmetric information. Traditional literature in management science typically addresses these information gaps using screening menus, strategic information sharing frameworks, or decentralized networks to reallocate bargaining power ( Cachon and Lariviere 2001 , Lu et al. 2006 , Nagarajan and Sošić 2008 , Lovejoy 2010 ) .
